title: Pot Luck Gari Foto
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: Built on half a tin of corned beef and scrambled egg — keep turning it until there are no dry white or yellow lumps of gari left.
longDesc: The store-cupboard version, and the cue at the end of it is the clearest statement anywhere of what garifoto should look like: keep turning it until the stew saturates the gari and there are no dry white or yellow lumps. Two cups of gari are dampened with three quarters of a cup of water and a quarter teaspoon of salt, sprinkled on with a fork, and the gari should be dampened but not dripping wet. Eggs are scrambled separately and set aside; onion, corned beef, garlic, tomatoes, ginger and red pepper cook in palm and peanut oil; the eggs go back in, then the gari on low heat.
ingredients: 2 large fresh tomatoes, or 2 cups grape tomatoes, chopped — or 3 drained tinned tomatoes, chopped, seeded if preferred
1/2 tin corned beef, about 6 oz — or 1 cup of any leftover fish, meat or beans, in chunks
6 tbsp peanut or other vegetable oil
2 tbsp red palm oil, if available
1 tsp fresh grated ginger, or 1/2 tsp dried ground ginger
steps: Sprinkle the water and salt over the gari with a fork. The gari should be dampened, but not dripping wet.
Scramble the eggs and set them aside.
Heat the palm and peanut oils.
Add the corned beef, garlic, tomatoes, ginger and red pepper.
Add the scrambled eggs back in.
Turn the heat to low and mix in the gari mixture, using a fork to break up any lumps of gari.
Keep turning it until the stew saturates the gari and there are no dry white or yellow lumps.
chefTips: The finishing cue is the best description of correctly made garifoto anywhere: keep turning until the stew saturates the gari and there are no dry white or yellow lumps. Dry lumps are the fault to look for.
Dampened but not dripping wet, sprinkled on with a FORK. A fork distributes the water far more evenly than pouring.
Scramble the eggs separately and add them back. Cracking eggs into the pan gives you a different dish.
Both oils — six tablespoons of peanut and two of palm. The palm oil is for colour and flavour rather than volume.
Half a tin of corned beef is what makes this a pot-luck dish, and she offers leftover fish, meat or beans as alternatives. It is a use-what-you-have recipe.
A fork again for breaking up lumps as the gari goes in. Gari clumps and a spoon will not separate it.
A fancier egg option she mentions is omelette strips rather than scrambled.
commonMistakes: Pouring the water on rather than sprinkling with a fork.
Cooking the eggs in the stew.
Leaving dry white lumps of gari in the finished dish.
Using only one of the two oils.
sources: Adapted from 'Recipe #3: Pot Luck Gari foto', betumi.com, carrying the copyright line '©Fran Osseo-Asare, 2009'. The post date is not printed beyond the day of the week. NOTE: this is one of the few pages on her sites where the SURNAME appears in a copyright line rather than only 'Fran' as a post byline. Ingredients TWO-PASS; the method was verbatim-matched on a third fetch.

Ingredients exactly as printed: 1 onion, chopped; 2 large fresh tomatoes, or 2 cups grape tomatoes, chopped (or 3 drained canned tomatoes, chopped), seeded if preferred; 1/2 tin of canned corned beef (or about 6 oz., or 1 cup of any leftover fish, meat, or beans), in chunks; 1 Tablespoon tomato sauce (optional); 6 Tablespoons of peanut or other vegetable oil; 2 eggs, beaten; 2 cups of gari; 3/4 cup water; 1/4 teaspoon salt; 2 Tablespoons red palm oil (if available); 1 teaspoon fresh grated ginger (or 1/2 teaspoon dried ground ginger); 1/4 teaspoon ground red pepper; 'parley' [sic] for garnish, optional; 1 or 2 cloves of garlic (optional). The misspelling 'parley' for parsley is as printed.

Method as printed: sprinkle the water-and-salt over the gari with a fork — 'The gari should be dampened, but not dripping wet.' Scramble the eggs and set aside. Heat palm and peanut oils; sauté onion until clear; add corned beef, garlic, tomatoes, ginger, red pepper; add the eggs.

THE FINISHING CUE, verbatim and the clearest in the garifoto record: 'Turn the heat to low and mix in the gari mixture, using a fork to break up any lumps of gari. Keep turning it until the stew saturates the gari and there are no dry white (or yellow) lumps.'
SINGLE-PASS detail: a 'fancy' omelette-strip egg option is also mentioned.
NO YIELD is printed. The four servings above is an editorial reading of two cups of gari.

THE DISAGREEMENT WITH THE OTHER DOCUMENTED VERSION, unreconciled: this one is built on CORNED BEEF with scrambled egg mixed through, uses 2 cups of gari to ¾ cup of water, and has no blanched vegetables at all. Selassie Atadika's (GHA055) is vegetarian and vegetable-led, uses 1½ cups of gari to ½ cup of water, blanches carrots, green beans and green pepper separately, and finishes with prekese, basil and a whole egg on top. The gari-to-water ratios are close — roughly 2.7:1 here against 3:1 — which is the one point of near-agreement. Neither recipe is corrected toward the other.
A NAMING NOTE from this author elsewhere: gari foto is sometimes called 'gari jollof' in Ghana.
FERMENTATION: none. Gari is a bought ingredient and its own production, which is a fermentation, is not published in this collection.
storage: 2 days refrigerated. It firms up as the gari keeps absorbing.
reheating: Low heat with a splash of water.
healthBenefits: Gari is gluten-free and supplies resistant starch.
Eggs and corned beef together make it high in complete protein.
Red palm oil provides provitamin-A carotenoids.
Uses up leftovers, which is the point of the dish.
culturalNote: Pot luck is exactly right as a name — gari foto is a dish for whatever is in the cupboard, and half a tin of corned beef is as authentic an ingredient in modern Ghanaian cooking as anything grown locally. The instruction to hunt down dry white lumps is the voice of someone who has eaten a badly made one.
